transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I guess what brings me in is that I’m really struggling to keep my attention on things I genuinely need to do. Like, I’m a secondary school teacher, so there’s a lot of reading and marking and planning, and I’ll sit down with a stack of essays or a curriculum document fully intending to get through it. I’ll have my pen out, maybe a cup of coffee, I’ll tell myself, “Right, just focus on this.”

And then ten minutes later I sort of come to and realize I’ve been staring at the same page the whole time. I’m not really absorbing what I’m reading. My eyes are moving over the words, but my mind is off thinking about three completely different things, and then I have to reread the same paragraph again and again. It’s frustrating because I’m not trying to avoid the work — I actually want to do it — but it’s like I can’t keep my mind on the thing in front of me for long enough to make proper progress.
Would you say you've had this kind of trouble focusing since you were a kid, or is this something that's really only become a problem more recently?

No, I don’t think it’s completely new. It’s definitely more obvious now because my job has so many things that rely on me sitting down and getting through work on my own, but when I think back, it was there when I was a kid too.

In primary school, my reports used to say things like I was “bright but careless,” or that I “didn’t finish work unless closely supervised.” I remember that phrase, or something like it, coming up more than once. At the time everyone sort of treated it like I was just not trying hard enough, or like I was a bit dreamy.

And my parents were always finding worksheets crumpled up in the bottom of my backpack that I’d done, or partly done, but forgotten to hand in. Not because I was trying to hide them — I’d just completely lose track of them. So yes, looking back, it does feel like the same kind of problem has been there since I was young, even if I didn’t really understand it that way then.
When your mind wanders off during these tasks, is it usually drifting toward worries or anxious thoughts about things going wrong, or does it just drift to random unrelated thoughts?

It’s usually not worry, no. I mean, I do get frustrated when I realize it’s happening, but the wandering itself is more… random, I suppose.

Like if I’m reading a curriculum document or marking essays, I’ll genuinely be trying to focus on the page, and then after a bit I realize I’m thinking about something completely unrelated — a conversation I had earlier, something I need to look up, an idea for a lesson, what I’m going to make for dinner, just all sorts of disconnected things. It’s not usually, “Oh no, this is going to go wrong,” or some spiral of anxious thoughts. It’s more like my mind has just slipped off the track without me noticing.

That’s the annoying part, really. I don’t always catch it straight away. I can be staring at the same paragraph for ten minutes, eyes moving over the words, and then realize I haven’t taken any of it in because I’ve been mentally somewhere else entirely.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a chronic, longstanding pattern of inattention—difficulty sustaining focus on tasks (reading, marking, planning), being easily distracted by unrelated internal thoughts, losing track of completed work, and needing external structure/supervision to finish tasks. These symptoms date back to childhood (documented as 'bright but careless,' 'didn't finish work unless closely supervised,' losing worksheets), fulfilling the childhood-onset requirement. The mind-wandering is described as random and unrelated to worry or anxious rumination, arguing against an anxiety disorder as the primary cause of inattention. There is no reported history of hyperactivity or impulsivity, supporting a predominantly inattentive presentation rather than combined type. Symptoms are currently causing functional impairment in occupational functioning (teacher struggling to complete essential job tasks). This pattern is most consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.
